Even though this boil-off management technology is used for the on-road transport section, there is likely to be some applicability of the technology in LH -powered aircraft systems. 2 4.2.2 Liquified Natural Gas Delivery, Storage, Dispensing, On-Site Liquification The most significant method of transporting LNG is marine shipping using purpose-built LNG carriers. These vessels employ double-hulled designs and advanced cryogenic containment systems such as Moss spherical tanks or membrane-type tanks. More discussion on this is available in Section 4.1.4. LNG carriers maintain low temperatures through insulation and by using boil-off gas as fuel for propulsion, with capacities ranging from about 125,000 to more than 260,000 cubic meters. The operation involves careful loading procedures at liquefaction terminals, long-distance transport across controlled shipping routes, and unloading at regasification terminals equipped with specialized cryogenic handling equipment. Although LNG itself cannot be transported through pipelines due to low temperature and liquid state, pipelines are vital components of LNG logistics. Before liquefaction, natural gas is transported via transmission pipeline networks to LNG plants. The liquefied gas (LNG) is distributed by ship or rail to the receiving terminal followed by regasification for distribution across smaller pipeline networks. These supply the gas continuously to consumers and supplement the distribution of the product by LNG shipping over long distances. Pipelines can be more economical for transport over land and operate with LNG infrastructure to provide a steady supply. Airports lacking pipeline infrastructure can also be supplied with LNG through specially designed road tankers that carry the fuel in vacuum-insulated, double-walled vessels at the low temperatures required. These tankers typically carry between 30 and 50 cubic meters and offer a very flexible method for keeping a consistent supply of LNG on hand. They would be suitable for smaller aviation fuel distribution chains, especially for regional airports and any places considering newer alternative fuel routes. With small or “micro-LNG” production facilities becoming more prevalent, road-based delivery has become an increasingly significant and scalable solution to meet the aviation-related LNG requirements. 71 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Beyond on-road delivery, it is also feasible for LNG supplies to be delivered to airports by rail in cryogenic tank cars or rail-compatible International Organization for Standardization (ISO) tank containers. Rail shipment can be especially valuable for supplying the numerous airports located a considerable distance inland, where building new pipelines is not workable, or alternatively when truck deliveries cannot meet the required fuel demand. Compared with on-road transport, rail has much greater capacity and improved efficiency of movement for large volumes of LNG. However, because of the cryogenic and flammable properties, transport requires very stringent safety and operational controls. LNG could also be supplied to airports through ISO standard tank containers, which are specifically designed for various transport modes like trucks, trains, and conventional container ships without necessarily depending on LNG-dedicated ships.
